title: Khara and Dushana
hook: the sages and the gods gather in the sky to watch one man stand in front of an army

segments.voice: Yesterday: fourteen thousand marched, and Rama sent Sita and Lakshmana to a cave. I'll face them alone.

Rama puts on his armor, strings his bow, and waits outside the empty hut. Valmiki says the sages, the gods and the celestial beings gather in the sky above Janasthana to watch. Some are worried: one man against fourteen thousand. They pray for him aloud. Then dust rises on the horizon, the drums grow louder, and Khara's army comes into view, a dark mass like storm clouds rolling in.
screen: `ARMOR ON, BOW STRUNG.` → `THE GODS WATCH FROM THE SKY.` → `AN ARMY LIKE STORM CLOUDS.`

segments.voice: Valmiki tells the battle over several chapters. Rama's arrows fly so fast, he says, that the rakshasas can't see him draw or release, only the bow bent into a circle. The army falls back, regroups, and charges again. Dushana leads one assault and falls. Trishiras, the three-headed, comes next, and falls too. Then only Khara is left, and their fight is fierce. Khara cuts Rama's bow and shatters his armor; Rama takes up another bow and goes on. Khara even tears up a tree and hurls it. They trade taunts, and Rama names what Khara has done: the sages terrorized, the hermits killed in the forest. At last Rama fits an arrow, and Khara falls. The text says it was over in a muhurta and a half, a little over an hour. The gods rain flowers, and the sages come down to praise him. Then Lakshmana brings Sita out of the cave, and Sita, seeing Rama alive and unhurt among grateful sages, runs and holds him. A few days ago, Rama promised the sages protection, and Sita asked whether that promise was wise. Today it's kept, at full cost, by one person. But one rakshasa, Valmiki says, slipped away. His name is Akampana, and he's heading south, toward the sea, toward Lanka.
screen: `THE BOW BENT INTO A CIRCLE.` · `DUSHANA FALLS, THEN TRISHIRAS.` · `KHARA AND RAMA, ALONE.` · `SITA RUNS TO HIM.` · then, large: `ONE ESCAPES TO LANKA.`

segments.voice: Let your body be still and alert, and think of a promise that turned out harder to keep than you expected. Picture yourself keeping it, or the part of it you still can, and breathe into any tiredness that comes. A kept promise doesn't need to be dramatic.
Muhurta. A traditional unit of time, about 48 minutes: Rama's battle alone against Khara's army takes a muhurta and a half, a little over an hour.
Your line: one escapes to Lanka. Tomorrow, the story crosses the sea to Ravana. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The battle of Janasthana is told in many Ramlila performances, and devotees often point to it as the moment Rama's promise to the forest sages is fulfilled.

original.note: Sanskrit muhūrta: a traditional unit of time, about 48 minutes. the battle takes one and a half, a little over an hour.

what a scholar hears: Aranya 25–30 end with Khara's death; the survivor Akampana carries the news to Ravana in Aranya 31.

chat.says: Rama against fourteen thousand? How did that battle end?
options: Rama won alone in about a muhurta and a half, but one rakshasa escaped to Lanka.
Lakshmana came out of the cave, and the two brothers won it together.
Khara surrendered and promised to leave the sages of the forest in peace.
chat.meaning: Rama defeated Dushana, Trishiras and Khara alone, in a little over an hour. Only Akampana slipped away, toward Lanka.

muhurta.meaning: a traditional unit of time, about 48 minutes

Janasthana.meaning: Khara's realm, where the battle is fought

Trishiras.meaning: the three-headed rakshasa in Khara's army

Akampana.meaning: the one rakshasa who escapes toward Lanka

Lanka.meaning: Ravana's island kingdom across the sea

recall: the sage who waited to see Rama

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 25–30 (the battle; Dushana, Trishiras and Khara fall; Sita embraces Rama)
Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 31 (Akampana escapes to Lanka)

notes: 'A little over an hour' renders 'a muhurta and a half' (1.5 x 48 minutes = 72 minutes; some editions differ); confirm.
Khara cutting Rama's bow and breaking his armor, and hurling a tree: confirm in Aranya 28–30.
The arrow that kills Khara is said in some editions to be one given by Agastya; left unspecified here.
